title: Fake Websites
about: Check a website's real name before you type anything in.

cards.prompt: A link in a text opens a page that looks just like your bank's. If it looks right, it's safe.
cards.explanation: False. A fake site can copy every logo and colour. Only the **address** shows who really owns the page.
cards.hint: What's easy to copy on a web page, and what isn't?
cards.nudge: Logos and colours are easy to copy. Something else tells you who owns the page.

cards.title: Read the address
cards.body:
A fake site can copy a logo, but not the real address. The **owner** is the name just before the **very last ending** (like `.example` or `.com.au`).

- `login.yourbank.example`: Your Bank's.
- `yourbank.example.login-check.example`: owned by **login-check.example**.
- `yourbank-secure.example`: a [[lookalike|lookalike-domain]].

cards.explanation: `yourbank.example/signin` and `login.yourbank.example` end in `yourbank.example`, so they're Your Bank's. The other two are lookalikes: the name isn't exactly `yourbank`.
cards.hint: For each one, find the very last ending and read the name just before it. Is that name exactly `yourbank`?
cards.nudge: Only the name just before the very last ending counts, and it must be exactly `yourbank`.

cards.sentence: A **padlock** means **encrypted**: nobody can read your data on its way to the site.

cards.prompt: This page has a padlock and wants your PIN. What does the padlock prove?

options.text: That the PIN can't be read on the way, whoever gets it
That the site was checked, so a PIN request is fine
options.nudge: Nobody checks a site's honesty before it gets a padlock. It's about the trip, not who's at the other end.

options.text: That it's your bank's page: scam sites can't get one
options.nudge: Scam sites can get a padlock too. Think about what encryption protects.

cards.explanation: A padlock only means nobody can read your data on the way. Scam sites can have one too, and a bank never asks for your PIN on a website.
cards.hint: Encryption protects your data on the trip. Does it tell you who's at the other end?

cards.prompt: Your Bank is `yourbank.example` and **never** asks for your PIN. Tap **every** warning sign.
cards.explanation: The address belongs to `login-check.example` (the **wrong owner**), the banner is **rushing you**, and it **asks for your card PIN**. The padlock and logo prove nothing.
cards.hint: Read the address to find its owner, then look for pressure and a secret.
cards.nudge: Look for who owns the address, pressure, and a secret, one at a time.

cards.prompt: Your **password manager** only fills in on the real site.

steps.text: The page looks right, but your **password manager doesn't offer to fill in** your password. What might that mean?

choices.text: This might not be the real site
choices.consequence: Good thinking. A password manager only fills in on the real address.

choices.text: The password manager is broken, so type it in
choices.consequence: The manager is working: it didn't recognise the address. Typing it in hands it over.

choices.text: Close it, then use the game's app or type the address
choices.consequence: Safe. If there was really something to sign in for, you'll see it there.

choices.text: Type it in just once, to check
choices.consequence: Once is enough for a fake site to keep your password.

cards.explanation: A quiet password manager is a clue the address isn't the real one. Sign in through the **app, a bookmark or the typed address**.
cards.hint: Where does a password manager fill in passwords? What's the safe way to reach an account?

cards.prompt: Oops. Before you noticed, you typed your bank password and card number into a fake site.

steps.text: What do you do about the password?

choices.text: Wait and see if anything strange happens
choices.consequence: Waiting gives the scammer time to use it. Fast is what counts.

choices.text: Change it straight away, and tell a trusted adult
choices.consequence: Now the stolen password is useless. And it's not your fault: fake sites fool adults too.

steps.text: Now the card. Which number do you call?

choices.text: The help number shown on the fake page
choices.consequence: That number belongs to the scammers. Use one you found yourself.

choices.text: The number on the card, or on the bank's official website
choices.consequence: The bank can stop the card before anyone uses it.

cards.explanation: **Change the password straight away** and tell a trusted adult. For a card, call the number **on the card or the bank's official website**, never one from the fake page.
cards.hint: What makes a stolen password useless? And where can you find a bank's number that a scammer didn't give you?

cards.prompt: Which address really belongs to Your Bank (`yourbank.example`)?

options.nudge: Find the very last ending, then the name just before it: `help-centre`. So help-centre.example owns it.
`yourbank-help` is a different name from `yourbank`: a lookalike.
`help-yourbank` isn't `yourbank`. Only the exact name before the ending counts.

cards.explanation: `help.yourbank.example` ends in `yourbank.example`: only the owner can add `help.` in front. The others belong to someone else.
cards.hint: For each address, find the very last ending, then the name just before it.

cards.title: Recap
cards.body:
- The **owner** is the name just before the very last ending.
- A **padlock only means encrypted**: scam sites can have one.
- **Try this:** bookmark the real sign-in pages you use.
